extraction.name: CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100
extraction.description: Two labeled subsets of the 80 million tiny images dataset. CIFAR-10 contains 6000 examples of each of 10 classes (airplane, automobile, bird, cat, deer, dog, frog, horse, ship, truck) for a total of 60000 images. CIFAR-100 contains 600 examples of each of 100 non-overlapping classes organized into 20 superclasses of five classes each. Both datasets consist of 32x32 colour images collected from the web and manually labeled by paid student annotators.
extraction.creator: Alex Krizhevsky
extraction.citeAs: Krizhevsky, A. (2009). Learning Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images. Technical Report.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Students were paid to label a subset of the 80 million tiny images dataset. Each labeler was given a class and asked to examine all images found with that class as the search term, as well as images found with hyponyms of the main search term (as defined by WordNet). Labelers were instructed to reject images that did not belong to their assigned class based on specific criteria. Every label submitted by the labelers was personally verified by the authors. Duplicate images were removed by comparing images with the L2 norm using a rejection threshold liberal enough to capture not just perfect duplicates but also re-saved JPEGs.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The 80 million tiny images dataset collected by groups at MIT and NYU, assembled by searching the web for images of every non-abstract English noun in the WordNet lexical database using several search engines including Google, Flickr, and Altavista, keeping roughly the first 3000 results for each search term. Images were downscaled to 32x32 colour images.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The underlying 80 million tiny images dataset was collected over the span of six months (exact dates not specified). The CIFAR labeling timeframe is not explicitly stated.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset was divided into a training set and test set, with the training set receiving a randomly-selected 5000 images from each class (for CIFAR-10). Duplicate images were removed using the L2 norm with a threshold liberal enough to capture perfect duplicates as well as re-saved JPEGs.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images were downscaled to 32x32 pixels. Duplicate images and images in which an excessively large portion of pixels were white were removed from the original 80 million tiny images dataset. For model training, ZCA whitening transformation was applied, and the 1000 least-significant directions of variance were deleted from the dataset.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Each labeler was given a class and asked to examine all images found with that class as the search term and with hyponym search terms. Labelers were instructed to reject images not belonging to their assigned class based on the following criteria: (1) the class name should be high on the list of likely answers to 'What is in this picture?'; (2) the image should be photo-realistic (line drawings rejected); (3) the image should contain only one prominent instance of the object; (4) the object may be partially occluded or seen from an unusual viewpoint as long as its identity is clear. Labelers were paid a fixed sum per hour. Every label submitted was personally verified by the authors.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Every label submitted by the labelers was personally verified by the authors. The instruction sheet specified that false positives (incorrectly included images) are worse than false negatives (incorrectly excluded images).
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Paid students (no further demographic details provided).
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The search term used to find an image provides it with a rough label, although it is extremely unreliable due to the nature of online image search technology. The original 80 million tiny images dataset contains noisy labels based on search terms.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The original tiny images dataset has no reliable class labels, which makes it hard to use for object recognition experiments. The labeled subsets (CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100) were created to address this. All experiments were performed with CIFAR-10 because CIFAR-100 was only very recently completed at the time of writing.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training and testing for object recognition and classification experiments. Used for unsupervised pre-training of generative models (RBMs and DBNs) and supervised classification with logistic regression and neural networks. CIFAR-100 classes can also be used as negative examples for CIFAR-10.
